title: Household shared shopping list: when a note is enough
summary: Explore clearer handoffs for shared households before building a general-purpose shared shopping app. The simulated planner sees conditional value in item ownership and acknowledgment on one list, while the solo shopper would retain a sufficient private note. Whether real households encounter enough handoff friction to justify switching remains untested.

findings.statement: A new list display alone gives neither simulated role a reason to switch: the shared note is sufficient for settled requests and one shopper, while the private note is sufficient for the solo role's essentials and open-ended choices.
limitations: Both baselines were deliberately assumed, not observed in real households.
The cited counterevidence bounds sufficiency: a handoff could create a coordination question and awkward note access could create a capture question; neither gap was established as an actual problem.

findings.statement: For the simulated shared planner, optional item assignment and visible acknowledgment on one canonical list are a candidate handoff benefit, conditional on the other adult participating and avoiding duplicate maintenance.
limitations: The same planner proposes initials and direct confirmation as a sufficient workaround, so feature interest does not establish a switching need.
Late-change frequency, actual confusion and the other adult's participation remain unknown. The second adult is a scenario condition, not an additional interviewed persona.

findings.statement: The simulated spontaneous solo shopper rejects sharing as a switching reason and rejects mandatory household setup or detailed planning. A private mode would be worth comparing only if capture becomes easier on the person's actual device while optional choices remain open.
limitations: The cited counterevidence limits any private-mode opportunity: the role would keep the already sufficient note when access stays easy.
Device, accessibility requirements and input method are explicit unknowns. No interface comparison or measured speed advantage exists.

next_steps: With consenting real shared households, observe how settled lists and late handoffs work using their current tools. Establish whether ownership ambiguity occurs and how often before prioritizing assignment features.

Compare a shared note with initials and direct confirmation against a single-list prototype with optional assignment and acknowledgment. Observe whether both adults can identify responsibility and whether maintenance effort increases; do not assume the prototype wins.

With real solo shoppers, compare adding an essential to their existing note against a private capture prototype on their own devices, accounting for accessibility needs. Ask whether leaving optional choices unplanned remains possible and accept retaining the note as a valid outcome.

If a later study needs to separate decision style from coordination, include weekly solo planners and spontaneous shared-household shoppers. Those two combinations are intentionally absent from this two-persona run.
limitations: All personas and answers are synthetic, not independent samples or observed customer evidence.
The two scenarios change both planning style and household coordination together, so their independent effects cannot be separated. Three-turn interviews leave many conditions unexplored.
Late-change frequency, device and accessibility needs remain unknown. Willingness to pay, adoption, retention and measured benefit have not been established.
Assignment, acknowledgment and private mode are hypothetical variants, not tested product capabilities.
